unit.title: Kana: Learning to Read Japanese
unit.summary: From no Japanese at all to reading both syllabaries and hearing the beat of the language. Kanji comes after this, not during it.

gate.message: Both kana have to come before anything else. Japanese written in romaji is not Japanese, and every hour spent reading it is an hour spent building a habit you will have to break.

lessons.title: Three alphabets, and why
objectives: Know what hiragana, katakana and kanji each do
Understand that kana is phonetic and learnable in days

steps.heading: Japanese uses three scripts at once
body: A single Japanese sentence normally contains all three. That sounds alarming and is not, because they divide the work cleanly.
**Hiragana** (ひらがな) is a phonetic alphabet of 46 basic characters. It writes grammar — the endings, the particles, the connective bits. Learn it first.

**Katakana** (カタカナ) is the same 46 sounds in a second set of shapes. It writes foreign words, names and emphasis. Because Japanese has borrowed heavily from English, katakana gives you hundreds of words almost free.
**Kanji** (漢字) are Chinese characters used for the meaningful cores of words. There are thousands, they are learned over years, and you do not need them to start.
Kana is phonetic and finite. Most learners read both sets within two weeks.

steps.heading: What a real sentence looks like
steps.body: 私は学校に行きます。 — 私 and 学校 and 行 are kanji carrying the meaning; は, に and きます are hiragana carrying the grammar.
steps.point: The kanji tell you what. The hiragana tell you how it fits together.

steps.heading: Katakana you can already almost read

items.english: bread — from Portuguese pão, not English

points: Hiragana for grammar, katakana for foreign words, kanji for meaning
Kana is phonetic and takes days, not years
Next: your first five sounds

lessons.title: The five vowels: あ い う え お
objectives: Read あいうえお
Understand that every Japanese sound is built on these five

steps.heading: Five vowels, and everything else is built from them
body: Japanese has exactly five vowel sounds. Not eleven like English — five, and they never change.

あ a — like the a in 'father'.
い i — like the ee in 'see'.
う u — like 'oo' but with your lips flat, not rounded.
え e — like the e in 'bed'.
お o — like the o in 'go', held steady.
Every other kana is one of these five with a consonant in front. か is k+a, き is k+i, and so on. Learn the five and the other forty become a grid you can predict.

steps.heading: The one that needs attention
body: う is not the English 'oo'. Say 'oo' and notice your lips push forward into a circle. Now do it again with your lips relaxed and flat. That is う.
It also frequently disappears. です sounds like 'des', not 'desu'. すき sounds like 'ski'. Do not fight this — pronouncing it fully sounds oddly formal.

points: Five vowels, never more
Every kana is a consonant plus one of these
う has flat lips and often drops out

lessons.title: か and さ rows
objectives: Read かきくけこ and さしすせそ
Know that し is shi, not si

steps.heading: The grid begins
body: か き く け こ is just k + each vowel. Nothing surprising.
さ し す せ そ is s + each vowel — except し, which is **shi**, not 'si'. That one is a genuine exception and it is very common: 私 (watashi), します (shimasu), 寿司 (sushi).

points: か-row and さ-row are regular
し is shi — the first real exception

lessons.title: た and な rows
objectives: Read たちつてと and なにぬねの
Know that ち is chi and つ is tsu

steps.heading: Two more exceptions, both common
body: た ち つ て と is t + vowel, except ち is **chi** and つ is **tsu**.

つ is the hardest single sound for English speakers. Put your tongue where it goes for 't', then release it into an 's' — ts, all in one motion. It is the sound at the end of 'cats', moved to the front of a syllable.
な に ぬ ね の is completely regular. A rest.

steps.note: つ first. Say 'cats', isolate the 'ts', then put a う on the end.

points: ち is chi, つ is tsu
な-row is regular
You can now read ねこ and いぬ

lessons.title: は, ま, や, ら, わ and ん
objectives: Finish the basic hiragana
Know ふ is fu and ん is its own beat

steps.heading: The last five rows
body: は ひ ふ へ ほ — ふ is **fu**, made with both lips rather than teeth on lip. Blow gently, as if cooling soup.
ま み む め も and や ゆ よ are regular. や-row has only three.
ら り る れ ろ — the tricky one. Not an English r and not an English l: a single quick tap of the tongue, like the middle of American 'butter'.
わ and を. を is pronounced exactly like お and survives only as the object particle.
ん is the only kana that is a consonant on its own — and it is a **full beat**, not a letter tacked onto the one before it.

steps.heading: は and へ lead a double life
body: When は is the topic particle it is read **wa**, not ha. When へ marks a direction it is read **e**, not he.
Inside ordinary words they are read normally: はな is hana, へや is heya.
This is a historical spelling that never got updated. Every learner trips on it once.

steps.note: Tap, do not curl. Say 'butter' quickly and isolate the tap.

points: All 46 basic hiragana covered
ふ uses both lips, ら-row is a tap
は is wa and へ is e as particles
ん is a full beat

lessons.title: Dakuten: two ticks change the sound
objectives: Read が ざ だ ば and ぱ rows
Understand the ticks as a system, not 25 new characters

steps.heading: Twenty-five sounds, zero new shapes
body: Add two small ticks (゛) to a kana and the consonant becomes voiced. か becomes が, さ becomes ざ, た becomes だ, は becomes ば.
Add a small circle (゜) to the は-row only and it becomes ぱ ぴ ぷ ぺ ぽ.
So you are not learning 25 new characters. You are learning one mark applied to shapes you already know.

steps.heading: Two pairs that sound identical
body: じ and ぢ are pronounced the same. So are ず and づ.
Modern Japanese uses じ and ず for almost everything; ぢ and づ survive in a handful of compounds like 鼻血 and 続く.
This is a spelling problem, not a listening one — learn which words take which.

points: ゛ voices the consonant; ゜ makes the p-row
じ/ぢ and ず/づ sound the same — a spelling matter

lessons.title: Small kana: ゃゅょ and っ
objectives: Read きゃ, しゅ, ちょ
Hear and produce the small っ
Count mora correctly
lessons.difficulty_warning: This lesson is where Japanese timing starts. Take it slowly — the beat matters more than the letters.

steps.heading: A small ゃ tucks into the kana before it
body: き + ゃ written small = きゃ, pronounced 'kya' — **one beat**, not two.
It only works after the i-column kana: き し ち に ひ み り ぎ じ び ぴ.
し and ち keep their exceptions: しゃ is 'sha', ちゃ is 'cha'.
The size is the whole difference. きや is two beats (ki-ya); きゃ is one (kya).

steps.heading: The small っ is a beat of silence
body: This one has no equivalent in English and it is the most-skipped sound in beginner Japanese.
がっこう is four beats: が — (silence) — こ — う. You stop, hold, and then continue.
The silence IS the sound. きて means 'come'; きって means 'stamp'. They are different words.
Tap the beats on a table while you say them. It works better than trying to hear it.

points: Small ゃゅょ merge into one beat with the kana before
Small っ is a full beat of silence
Japanese timing is counted in beats, not letters

lessons.title: Katakana: the same sounds, new shapes
objectives: Read katakana
Use ー for long vowels
Read loanwords

steps.heading: No new sounds — only new shapes
body: Katakana covers exactly the same 46 sounds as hiragana. あ and ア are both 'a'.
It is used for words borrowed from other languages, foreign names, animal and plant names in science writing, onomatopoeia, and for emphasis — roughly where English uses italics.
The shapes are more angular. Several are easy to confuse: シ and ツ, ソ and ン. The trick is stroke direction — シ and ン are written from the bottom up, ツ and ソ from the top down.

steps.heading: The long vowel mark
body: Katakana uses ー to hold a vowel for a second beat. コーヒー is ko-o-hi-i: four beats.
This matters. ビル is a building; ビール is a beer. One beat apart.

points: Same sounds, angular shapes
ー holds a vowel for another beat
Watch シ/ツ and ソ/ン — stroke direction tells them apart

lessons.title: Reading real Japanese
lessons.title_ja: 読めるようになりました
objectives: Read unfamiliar kana at speed
Count mora reliably
Pass the kana gate

steps.instruction: Read each aloud, counting the beats.
items: ありがとうございます

steps.heading: Your first paragraph
steps.text: はじめまして。わたしはリティシです。にほんごをべんきょうしています。よろしくおねがいします。
steps.translation: Nice to meet you. I'm Rithish. I'm studying Japanese. Please treat me kindly.
steps.note: Written entirely in hiragana so you can read every character. Real Japanese would use kanji for わたし and にほんご — that comes next.
tasks: Count the beats in にほんご
Find the は that is read wa

on_pass.message: かなマスター. You can read Japanese. Kanji is next, and it gets easier from here because you can finally look things up.

on_fail.message: Not yet — and that is normal. The kana you missed are going into your review queue. Come back tomorrow.

points: You can read both kana
You can count mora, which is what makes you understandable
Romaji now switches off — you no longer need it
Next: kanji, and your first real sentences
